item.title: Organization of neuropeptide signaling: cross-species insights from small model organisms.
item.author: Zandawala M, Filosa A, Beets I.
item.description:
Neuropeptides are ancient signaling molecules that modulate neural circuit function and behavior across the animal kingdom. Model organisms such as Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and zebrafish serve as powerful in vivo models for deciphering the organization of neuropeptidergic signaling, owing to their smaller nervous systems, genetic tractability, and the growing availability of neural connectomes. In this article, we review how these organisms have advanced current understanding of neuropeptidergic transmission across three interconnected themes: (i) the roles of peptides in sensory-motor transformations, (ii) the conservation and divergence of peptidergic expression and network architecture across species, and (iii) the diversity of neurotransmission strategies employed by single neurons. item.title: An insular-orbitofrontal pathway supporting awareness of respiratory effort.
item.author: Jelinčić V, von Leupoldt A.
item.description:
In a recent study using human intracranial EEG recordings during inspiratory loading, Assi and colleagues identified parallel pathways for respiratory compensation and awareness. The anterior insula signals a neuromechanical mismatch to the orbitofrontal cortex for conscious appraisal, while high-frequency insular-frontal coupling enables ventilatory adjustments. The findings are highly relevant for disorders of altered respiratory perception.

item.title: Tumor innervation in non-central nervous system tumors: origins, mechanisms, and phenotypic plasticity.
item.author: Zhang Y, Ye Z, Wang Y, Tang S, Chen G.
item.description:
The peripheral nervous system has emerged as an important regulator of solid tumor biology. We synthesize recent advances in cancer neuroscience, focusing on three interconnected themes: the cellular origins of tumor-associated nerves, the molecular mechanisms that govern neural recruitment and remodeling, and the resulting phenotypic plasticity within the tumor microenvironment. Tumor innervation arises through axon extension from pre-existing nerves, recruitment of neural precursors, and neuron-like transdifferentiation of non-neuronal cells. These processes are driven by neurotrophic factors, axon guidance cues, extracellular vesicles, and stress-associated pathways. item.title: Apolipoprotein E4 and immune dysfunction in Alzheimer's disease: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
item.author: Shi H, Zhao Y, Zhu W, Wang YJ, Bu XL.
item.description:
Emerging evidence suggests that apolipoprotein E4 (APOE4) functions as an organizer of brain-periphery immune crosstalk, coupling maladaptive microglial states with peripheral immune remodeling to establish a self-reinforcing neuroimmune loop that may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease. In the central nervous system, APOE4 pushes microglia away from homeostatic surveillance toward metabolically stressed, inflammatory, and synaptotoxic phenotypes, thereby weakening pathological protein clearance and promoting neurodegeneration. In the periphery, APOE4 primes innate and adaptive immune cells toward a pro-inflammatory state, creating a reservoir that can communicate with the diseased brain and infiltrate it. item.title: Resilience and vulnerability in the midbrain dopamine system during aging.
item.author: McMurtrie G, Mabry SJ, Glausier JR, Rocha EM, Freyberg Z.
item.description:
The midbrain dopamine system is integral to movement, reward, and motivation, and its dysfunction underlies a range of brain disorders. Age is a primary risk factor for many of these disorders, yet systematic analysis of how the dopamine system changes during healthy aging remains relatively understudied. In this review, we first examine the impact of healthy aging on the dopamine system across sexes and species, including flies, mice, rats, and humans. We next consider the neuroadaptive mechanisms that sustain dopamine neuron function with age. Finally, we contrast the molecular mechanisms of age-related neurodegenerative diseases with those of healthy aging, exploring the possibility that loss of neuroadaptive reserve drives dopamine neurodegeneration. item.title: A brain circuit linking sleep loss to pain.
item.author: Li M, Yang G.
item.description:
Sleep loss heightens pain sensitivity, but the brain circuits involved remain unclear. In a recent study, Huang, Wang, Jiao, and colleagues identified a pathway connecting the retrosplenial cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and zona incerta that contributes to heightened sensitivity to mechanical stimulation and heat after sleep deprivation in male mice.

item.title: The mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome in aging and brain diseases.
item.author: Shawky AA, Huang HT, Parikh D, Morris-Blanco KC.
item.description:
The mitochondrial genome is a dynamic regulatory platform that extends far beyond its protein-coding capacity. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) harbors epigenetic modifications and produces diverse noncoding RNAs that influence mitochondrial function and cellular homeostasis. Evidence from animal models and human studies indicates that mtDNA methylation, mitochondrial-encoded noncoding RNAs, and cytosolic release of mitochondrial nucleic acids regulate transcription, metabolism, and stress signaling. Furthermore, these mechanisms are altered in aging, neurodegenerative disease, and acute brain injury. In this review, we synthesize emerging insights into how the mitochondrial epigenome and noncoding genome shape mitochondrial function and serve as regulatory interfaces linking cellular stress and neuronal vulnerability in brain aging and disease.

item.title: Interpersonal neural synchrony: one label, many phenomena.
item.author: Novembre G, Koul A, Bigand F.
item.description:
Brains synchronize interpersonally during social interaction, yet the term 'synchrony' is often used to describe phenomena with different origins and functional implications. In this article, we briefly synthesize and organize these phenomena according to their signal and coupling properties, highlighting the value of disambiguation for reproducibility, theoretical clarity, and translational impact.

item.title: Sleep-dependent microglial functions in Alzheimer's disease.
item.author: Calafate S, Mancuso R.
item.description:
Sleep is a fundamental regulator of brain homeostasis, yet how distinct brain cell types contribute to this process remains poorly understood. Microglia, the resident immune cells of the central nervous system, actively regulate neuroinflammatory tone, metabolic waste clearance, and synaptic remodeling, thereby contributing to neural circuit maintenance and proteostasis. Delineating the different functions played by microglia during specific brain states, such as sleep, represents an active area of research. In this article, we review a growing literature supporting the notion that sleep dynamically shapes microglial functional outputs.
